cases.question: For a classic Stellar asset, how do burning, clawback, and redemption differ mechanically, and do tokens return to the issuer?

golden.answer:
For a classic issued asset, the issuer account is the asset's authority, not a normal holder of its own credit. Stellar's asset docs state that an asset is created by an issuing account payment and that deleting or burning an issued asset is done by sending it back to the issuing account. The SAC docs make the same accounting explicit: transfers to the issuer account burn, while transfers from the issuer mint. That is the mechanical basis for voluntary redemption: a holder pays the issuer/distributor according to the issuer's redemption process, and the asset balance is removed from outstanding holder balances.

Clawback is different. Under CAP-35 and the Stellar control-access docs, an issuer can claw back only assets/trustlines that were clawback-enabled under the required flags. The issuer submits a clawback operation against the holder's balance; the SAC interface describes the clawed-back amount as burned in the clawback process. It is not a normal user payment, does not require the affected holder's signature, and does not create a spendable issuer balance.

So: redemption/payment back to the issuer is holder-initiated and usually part of off-chain cash settlement; burn is the supply/accounting effect of returning issued credit to the issuer; clawback is issuer-initiated removal under regulated-asset controls.
keyFacts: Identifies non-issuer classic balances as issued supply.
Treats classic asset returns to the issuer as redemption/burn-like.
Clawback removes a holder balance under clawback-enabled issuer controls.
Distinguishes voluntary redemption/payment back to issuer from issuer-initiated clawback.
avoid: Do NOT say the issuer holds its own classic asset as a normal balance.
Do NOT say clawed-back classic-asset tokens become a spendable issuer balance.
Do NOT conflate user redemption with issuer clawback authorization.
Do NOT detour into per-transfer fee hooks, max-supply caps, or the full AUTH_* flag enumeration; the question is the burn/clawback/redemption distinction.

cases.question: How do I find all Stellar claimable balances addressed to me, claim one or several by id, and confirm none remain?

golden.answer:
Discover first, then claim by balance id. On Horizon, use the claimable-balances collection and filter for the claimant account, then page through the result set until exhausted. Each record has a claimable-balance id and claimants/predicates. A single claimable balance can also be retrieved by `/claimable_balances/:claimable_balance_id`.

To claim, the claimant account submits one `ClaimClaimableBalance` operation per balance id, with the claimant account as the operation source. Multiple claim operations can be placed in one transaction if the transaction size/operation limits and account sequence handling allow it. The protocol operation adds the claimable-balance amount to the source account and deletes the claimable-balance entry on success.

A listed balance is not necessarily claimable at this ledger close. The operation fails with `CLAIM_CLAIMABLE_BALANCE_CANNOT_CLAIM` if no claimant matches the source account or the matched claimant's predicate is false. For non-native assets, the claiming account also needs the relevant trustline, enough remaining trustline limit, and required authorization. After the transaction confirms, query the claimant filter again and verify the claimed ids are absent and no remaining balances match.

cases.question: How do Stellar claimable-balance predicates, expiry, multi-claimant patterns, cancellation/reclaim patterns, and reserve costs work — e.g. if I list myself as a claimant, can I reclaim the balance anytime?

golden.answer:
A claimable balance contains an amount, an asset, a creator, and up to 10 claimants. Each claimant is an account plus a `ClaimPredicate`; that claimant can claim only when its predicate is true. Supported predicate shapes include unconditional, AND, OR, NOT, before absolute time, and before relative time. The docs also show after-time windows by negating a before-time predicate.

Expiry is not automatic deletion. A common expiring-payment design is: recipient claimant can claim before a deadline; sender/creator claimant can claim after the deadline. After the deadline, someone still has to submit the claim operation from the reclaim claimant to consume the entry. If no predicate ever becomes usable by a real claimant, the claimable balance can be stranded.

If you list yourself (the sender/creator) as a claimant, that does NOT give you an at-will reclaim right: you can only claim when your own predicate evaluates true, and listing yourself never overrides another claimant's predicate. A claimable balance is not a custodial balance the creator can pull back at will, and the predicate set — not an issuer clawback flag — is the control surface. (Issuer clawback under CAP-35 is a separate regulated-asset feature, not the creator's ordinary reclaim mechanism.)

Reserve matters for high-volume or long-lived designs. Creating a claimable balance increases the creator's minimum balance by one base reserve per claimant, and the Stellar lumens docs describe claimable balances as ledger entries that require a base reserve per claimant. The reserve is released when the entry is consumed.
keyFacts: Pairs each claimant with a predicate.
Requires the claimant's predicate to be true at claim time.
Uses before/after absolute or relative time predicates for expiry or reclaim windows.
Mentions each claimable balance consumes reserve while it exists.
avoid: Do NOT claim claimable balances expire automatically without a claim/reclaim operation removing them.
Do NOT say the creator can always claw back or cancel a claimable balance at will.
Do NOT conflate claimable-balance predicates with asset issuer clawback flags.

cases.question: As a Stellar asset issuer, can I charge transfer fees, cap supply, or freeze a holder, and what is actually possible at the protocol level?

golden.answer:
Classic Stellar assets do not have a protocol-level per-transfer issuer-fee hook like a custom token tax. They are identified by asset code plus issuer account, held on trustlines, and moved with Stellar payment/path-payment/offer operations. If an issuer needs custom transfer logic, that is a separate Soroban/custom-token design question, not a classic asset flag.

Supply caps are operational for classic assets. The issuer can stop minting, lock or disable issuer signing authority, and document supply commitments, but there is no immutable max-supply field attached to an arbitrary issued asset. (Supply is tracked as outstanding balances held outside the issuer; the burn/redemption accounting itself is covered separately in q-aas-burn-clawback-redemption-mechanics.)

Freeze and clawback are protocol controls, but only when configured correctly. `AUTH_REQUIRED_FLAG` requires authorization before holding/transacting; `AUTH_REVOCABLE_FLAG` lets the issuer deauthorize trustlines; `AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED_FLAG` allows clawback for subsequent clawback-enabled trustlines and requires revocable authorization. Freezing/deauthorization blocks use; clawback removes/burns a specified amount under CAP-35. These controls are holder-risk and decentralization tradeoffs, not hidden transfer fees.
keyFacts: Classic Stellar assets omit a built-in per-transfer issuer fee hook.
Classic asset supply caps use operational/governance controls.
The issuer can stop minting or lock/disable issuer control.
Authorization flags can authorize or deauthorize trustlines.
Clawback-enabled assets can claw back balances under the required flags.
avoid: Do NOT claim classic Stellar assets have a custom smart-contract tax.
Do NOT claim the protocol encodes an immutable max-supply field for arbitrary issued assets.
Do NOT claim classic Stellar assets can arbitrarily tax every transfer at the protocol level.
Do NOT claim clawback/freeze is available unless the relevant flags and trustline authorization model are in place.
Do NOT re-derive the full burn/redemption accounting (transfers-to-issuer-burn); reference clawback as an issuer control and stay on the fee/cap/freeze feasibility question.
golden.notes:
Verified flags and issuer-control boundaries against control-asset-access and CAP-35 (live 2026-06-29). Transfer-fee absence is inferred from the classic asset operation model and SAC docs rather than a single explicit negative statement. Differentiated from q-aas-burn-clawback-redemption-mechanics: this file owns the fee/cap/freeze feasibility debunk and AUTH_* enumeration and now references rather than re-derives burn accounting.
Also good if the answer: Distinguishes freezing/deauthorization from clawback and from burning/redeeming supply. | Mentions Soroban custom tokens could encode different token logic, but that is separate from classic asset issuer flags/SAC behavior.
Golden cites: Stellar docs on asset authorization flags/clawback and classic asset issuance.

cases.question: After issuing a Stellar asset, how do I make it tradable and visible on exchanges, wallets, explorers, and aggregators?

golden.answer:
Issuing a Stellar asset makes it technically valid, not automatically visible, trusted, liquid, or listed. The durable prerequisites are: issue the asset from the correct issuer account, make trustlines possible for holders, set the issuer account's `home_domain`, and publish a valid SEP-1 `https://DOMAIN/.well-known/stellar.toml` with `[[CURRENCIES]]` metadata for the exact code and issuer. SEP-1 says clients and exchanges can use that information to decide whether a token should be listed.

Tradability requires markets. On Stellar that can mean SDEX offers, liquidity pools, or integrations/listings in wallets, explorers, exchanges, and aggregators. Visibility and pricing usually require enough real liquidity, supply/issuer metadata, and a venue-specific policy review. SEP-42/Stellar Asset Lists define a community asset-list format and catalog that apps may use, but the catalog itself warns that inclusion in a list is not an endorsement or recommendation.

The practical answer is therefore a checklist, not a guarantee: publish correct SEP-1 metadata; keep issuer/domain/logo/contact/reserve information consistent; create real markets; apply to each target venue using its current listing process; and keep dated evidence for any verification, market-cap, or safety claim.
keyFacts: Requires asset issuance and trustlines.
Requires a home domain, valid SEP-1 metadata, logo, and issuer details.
Tradability needs SDEX offers, AMM pools, or wallet/exchange/aggregator listings.
These services set their own listing, verification, and liquidity policies.
avoid: Do NOT guarantee listing, verification, price, or market-cap display just because a Stellar asset exists.
Do NOT claim an official universal Stellar whitelist governs every exchange or aggregator.
golden.notes:
Freshness-sensitive. Verified durable prerequisites with SEP-1 and SEP-42; do not require any specific exchange/aggregator policy beyond dated current-source citation. Re-verified 2026-06-29: SEP-0042 confirmed as 'Stellar Asset List (SAL)', SEP-0001 + the build/apps SEP-1 tutorial resolve; stellar.expert/asset-lists is a client-rendered SPA so its catalog couldn't be content-fetched but the route is valid (load-bearing SEP claims verified via the protocol repo).

Golden cites: SEP-1 or Stellar asset docs, plus dated venue/listing sources for freshness-specific claims.

cases.question: What is SEP-30, and how does its recovery-signer-server model let a Stellar wallet recover accounts without holding the user's key?

golden.answer:
SEP-30 is Stellar's account-recovery standard for wallets that want users to regain access after losing a private key without giving a third party custody of that key. The official Wallet SDK docs describe the flow as a wallet communicating with one or more recovery signer servers to register the wallet for later recovery.

The mechanism relies on Stellar account signers and thresholds. Before loss, the wallet/account must be configured so recovery signer server(s) can participate in replacing signers or helping the user regain high-threshold control according to the SEP-30 flow. The recovery server verifies authenticated requests, commonly with SEP-10 JWTs or an external identity provider depending on the endpoint, and coordinates recovery. It does not need to hold the user's master secret key.

This is not a magic reset for arbitrary accounts. If the account was never enrolled with the right signers/thresholds, SEP-30 cannot recover it after the secret key is gone. It is also distinct from newer smart-account/passkey recovery patterns; SEP-30 is a classic-account signer-server standard.
keyFacts: Names SEP-30 as Stellar's account recovery standard using recovery signer servers.
Names the recovery server as a signer or signer-change coordinator.
States that the server need not hold the user's master secret key.
Grounds recovery in account signers, thresholds, and a wallet-server flow.
avoid: Do NOT claim SEP-30 can recover any Stellar account after the secret key is lost with no prior signer setup.
Do NOT say the recovery server should custody the user's master secret.
golden.notes:
SEP-30 spec status is Draft; official Wallet SDK docs still document the flow. Phase 3 can verify current Wallet SDK endpoint details if needed.
Also good if the answer: Notes multiple recovery methods or servers can be used depending on account setup and wallet support. | Distinguishes SEP-30 recovery from passkey smart-account recovery patterns.
Golden cites: SEP-30 specification or official Stellar docs covering recoverable wallets.

cases.question: Is there an official list of trusted Stellar assets or an SDK helper, and how should a wallet build a token whitelist to filter scam assets?

golden.answer:
There is no protocol-level official whitelist that makes a Stellar asset trusted across all wallets and apps. A Stellar asset can be valid on-chain while still being hidden, warned, unverified, or blocked by a particular wallet/explorer policy.

There is, however, a standards-based allowlist mechanism. SEP-42 defines Stellar Asset Lists: curated lists of Stellar asset metadata that applications can choose to trust. The community-managed `stellar-asset-lists/index` catalog and StellarExpert asset-list page let apps discover lists, and the `@stellar-asset-lists/sdk` package can fetch and parse them. The catalog explicitly says inclusion in a list should not be treated as endorsement or recommendation.

A wallet whitelist should combine sources and policy: exact asset code + issuer, issuer account and `home_domain`, SEP-1 TOML metadata and organization docs, known project/issuer sources, liquidity/market behavior, user reports or denylist evidence, and dated reviews of asset-list providers. SDK helpers can read metadata or SAL lists; they cannot certify that an asset is safe by themselves.

cases.question: How does a Stellar trustline limit work, what causes op_invalid_limit, and how do I safely remove a trustline without losing tokens?

golden.answer:
A trustline is the ledger entry that lets an account hold a non-native Stellar asset. Its `limit` is the maximum balance that account is willing/able to hold for that asset; changing the limit is done with `ChangeTrust`.

`op_invalid_limit` / `CHANGE_TRUST_INVALID_LIMIT` means the requested new limit is not sufficient to hold the current balance and buying liabilities. The operation docs explicitly call out the common removal case: trying to remove a trustline while it still has a nonzero asset balance. Other lifecycle constraints can also matter, such as missing issuer, low reserve, deauthorization, or liquidity-pool references.

To remove a trustline safely, first reduce the asset balance to zero through payment, trade, redemption/burn to issuer, or another valid disposition. Cancel or settle relevant offers/liabilities. Then submit `ChangeTrust` with limit `0`. When the trustline closes, the associated base reserve becomes available again; until then, the trustline increases the account's minimum XLM balance.
keyFacts: Explains a trustline limit caps the maximum balance the account can hold for that asset.
Defines `op_invalid_limit` as a new trustline limit outside protocol constraints.
Names a below-balance limit as a common `op_invalid_limit` cause.
Requires a zero asset balance before trustline removal.
Removes a trustline by setting its limit to zero.
avoid: Do NOT tell users to remove a trustline while it still has a nonzero balance.
Do NOT imply a trustline limit increases automatically without a Change Trust operation.
golden.notes:
Verified against operation docs and Horizon result-code docs.
Also good if the answer: Mentions trustlines increase the account minimum balance/reserve while present. | Notes authorization flags can affect whether the account can hold or transact the asset.

A wallet or cash-out provider may use downstream anchor rails, but those rails are optional, provider- and region-specific receiver choices rather than SDP's universal architecture. cases.question: What fee does a Stellar AMM liquidity pool charge per swap, and how many base reserves does a pool-share trustline require?

golden.answer:
A Stellar AMM liquidity pool charges a **fixed 30 basis points (0.30%)** fee per swap, and a
**pool-share trustline requires 2 base reserves** (vs. 1 for a regular asset trustline) [1]. Pools
enforce the **constant-product invariant `Asset A * Asset B = k`** — the protocol never lets the
product of the reserves decrease — and the 0.30% fee accrues into the pool, growing `k` so it is
distributed to liquidity providers proportional to their shares [1]. Pool shares are not

cases.question: What is a claimable balance on Stellar and when would you use one instead of a direct payment?

golden.answer:
A **claimable balance** is a native ledger entry that **sets aside an amount of an asset for one or
more designated claimants to claim later**, rather than sending it directly to an account. It is
created with the **`CreateClaimableBalance`** operation and redeemed with **`ClaimClaimableBalance`**
[1]. Each claimant can carry a **claim predicate** — e.g. time bounds (claimable after/before a
date), or unconditional — letting you express conditional/deferred transfers and simple escrow-like
payouts **without any smart contract / Soroban** [1].

Use it instead of a direct payment when **the recipient can't accept the payment yet** — most
commonly when they **have not established a trustline** to a non-native asset, or for
**predicate-gated / time-locked payouts** and airdrops where the sender wants to commit funds now
and let the recipient claim on their own terms [1]. The entry **holds a base reserve** (sponsored
by the creator) until claimed. Note: it is a **native protocol feature, not a Soroban escrow
contract**, and for a **non-native** asset the claimant must still have (or establish) a trustline
to that asset to claim it.

Source: [1] developers.stellar.org Claimable Balances docs.

cases.question: Walk me through issuing a new custom token on Stellar from scratch.

golden.answer:
There is **no 'create asset' operation** — a classic asset is defined by its **`(asset_code, issuer account)`** pair and simply comes into existence the first time the issuer pays it out [1][2]. The flow:

1. Create/fund the **issuing account** and a separate **distribution account** (two-account best practice) [1].
2. Optionally set issuer **authorization flags** first (e.g. AUTH_REQUIRED/REVOCABLE, or clawback) — these only apply to trustlines created afterward [1].
3. The **distribution account opens a trustline** to the asset via **`ChangeTrust`** [2].
4. The **issuer sends** (a `Payment`) the desired supply to the distribution account — this is the issuance/mint [2].
5. Publish a **`stellar.toml` (SEP-1)** so wallets can discover and identify the asset [1].
6. Optionally cap supply by locking the issuer (set master weight to 0 / AUTH_IMMUTABLE) [1].
keyFacts: A classic asset is defined by its asset code and issuing account.
The asset exists after the issuer sends it to an account with a trustline.
The distribution account establishes the asset trustline with ChangeTrust.
The issuer sends the supply to the distribution account with a Payment.
avoid: Do NOT describe issuing a Stellar asset as deploying a Solidity/ERC-20 contract.
Do NOT claim there is a dedicated 'createAsset' operation on the protocol.

cases.question: How do path payments work on Stellar and which two operations implement them?

golden.answer:
A **path payment** converts one asset into another in a **single atomic transaction**, routing
across the **Stellar DEX orderbook and/or AMM liquidity pools** to find a path — so the sender pays
in one asset and the recipient receives a different one, and neither party has to hold the
intermediate asset (this is what enables on-chain FX, e.g. USDC → EURC) [1]. Two operations
implement it [1]:

- **`PathPaymentStrictSend`** — the sender fixes the **exact source amount**; the recipient receives
  **at least `destMin`** of the destination asset.
- **`PathPaymentStrictReceive`** — the recipient is guaranteed an **exact destination amount**; the
  sender pays **at most `sendMax`**.

It settles in roughly one ledger close (~5 s) at the normal low network fee — no off-chain bridge or
third-party DEX router is involved.

Source: [1] developers.stellar.org path-payments / liquidity-on-the-Stellar-DEX docs.
keyFacts: Names both path-payment operations: PathPaymentStrictSend and PathPaymentStrictReceive.
Converts one asset to another through a path payment.
Routes through the DEX order book, AMM pools, or both.
Executes the routed payment atomically in one transaction.
avoid: Do NOT invent operation names (e.g. 'PathSwapOp', 'CrossAssetPaymentOp') as the canonical ops.
Do NOT claim path payments require an off-chain bridge or a third-party DEX router.
golden.notes:
Dossier §3.2. Two ops: PathPaymentStrictSend / PathPaymentStrictReceive. Verified against developers.stellar.org path-payments / liquidity docs.

cases.question: Compare the Stellar DEX (SDEX) orderbook with Stellar's AMM liquidity pools — how do they price trades and what are the cost differences?

golden.answer:
- **SDEX** is an on-chain **central-limit orderbook**: accounts post offers via `ManageBuyOffer`/`ManageSellOffer`/`CreatePassiveSellOffer`; matching is on-ledger and atomic. Offers can be priced **tighter or wider** at the maker's discretion [1].
- **AMM liquidity pools** price via a **constant-product (x·y=k)** curve; each swap charges a **fixed 30 basis points (0.30%)** fee, separate from the network fee. Fees accrue into the pool (growing `k`) and are paid out to LPs proportional to their pool shares [1].
- Both live **in-ledger (no off-chain matching engine)**, and a single **path payment** can route across **both** offers and pools in one atomic transaction [1].
- **AMM pool-share trustlines cost two base reserves** (vs one for a normal asset trustline). High-volume pairs tend to concentrate on offers; exotic/long-tail pairs on pools [1].

cases.question: What is a trustline on Stellar and what does it cost to hold an asset?

golden.answer:
- A **trustline** is an explicit **opt-in** (created with **`ChangeTrust`**) for an account to hold a specific non-native asset from a given issuer; it records the holder's balance and limit for that `(asset_code, issuer)` [1].
- **Without a trustline, payments of that asset fail/bounce** — the account cannot receive an asset it has not trusted [1].
- A trustline raises the account's minimum balance by **one base reserve (0.5 XLM)** — this is a held minimum, not a spent fee [2]. **Pool-share (AMM) trustlines cost two base reserves (1.0 XLM)**.
- **XLM (native) needs no trustline**; only non-native assets require one [1].
keyFacts: Defines a trustline as an account's explicit opt-in to hold a non-native asset.
Creates the trustline through ChangeTrust for a specific asset and issuer.
Without a trustline, payments of that asset fail/bounce.
Requires the account to keep enough XLM for each trustline's extra base reserve.
avoid: Do NOT claim assets can be received without any trustline (like ERC-20 on Ethereum).
Do NOT state the base reserve is a flat fee that is consumed/spent rather than a held minimum balance.
golden.notes:
Foundational. Dossier §1.2. Base reserve = 0.5 XLM; trustline = 1 base reserve; pool-share trustline = 2.
Also good if the answer: Each trustline reserves one base reserve (0.5 XLM). | Pool-share (AMM) trustlines cost two base reserves.
Golden cites: A trustlines page on developers.stellar.org.

cases.question: What's the difference between holding a classic Stellar asset via a trustline and the same asset through its Stellar Asset Contract (SAC)?

golden.answer:
They are **two views of the same asset, not two different tokens.** Holding a classic asset means
your account has a **trustline ledger entry** to `<code:issuer>`; the **Stellar Asset Contract
(SAC)** is a **protocol-reserved contract** that exposes that *same* classic asset to Soroban so
contracts can move it by contract ID [1]. There is **no separate "USDC-on-Soroban"** to migrate to
or hold alongside — one source of truth backs both [1].

- **Classic / trustline:** balances live in trustline entries; payments use classic operations and
  respect issuer auth flags. Each trustline costs a base reserve.
- **SAC:** a Soroban contract calls `transfer`/`balance`/etc. on the asset's SAC by contract ID;
  account balances still resolve to the underlying **trustline**, while contract-to-contract
  movements use **contract-data** entries [1].
- Both share one supply; the SAC implements **CAP-46-6** and the **SEP-41** token interface; the
  **issuer stays admin** (mint/clawback/set_authorized are issuer-only) [1].

You never redeploy, bridge, or wrap the asset to use it in Soroban.

Source: [1] developers.stellar.org Stellar Asset Contract page.
keyFacts: The SAC is a protocol-reserved contract for the same classic asset.
It exposes that classic asset to Soroban.
Classic holdings use trustline ledger entries.
The SAC lets Soroban contracts move the asset by contract ID.
Contract-to-contract transfers use contract data entries.
avoid: Do NOT claim the SAC is a distinct token requiring users to migrate balances or hold two versions of the asset.
Do NOT claim you must redeploy/bridge the asset to use it in Soroban.
golden.notes:
Required comparison (trustline vs SAC). Dossier §2, §8.1. Verified against developers.stellar.org SAC page.

cases.question: What's the recommended account structure for issuing a custom asset on Stellar, and why?

golden.answer:
- Recommended structure is **two accounts**: a separate **issuing account** and a **distribution account** [1].
- The **issuing account** mints supply by sending the asset, but it cannot hold a balance of its own asset. It manages authorization flags, should be **locked down / cold storage**, and should be used rarely. The **distribution account** is the public-facing account that sends the asset to users and holds a working float [1].
- Rationale is **blast-radius / segregation of duties**: if the hot distribution account is compromised, only the **float** is at risk, not the total supply, and the issuer retains flag/clawback control [1].
- Assets are defined by the **`(asset_code, issuer)`** pair, and holders need a **trustline**; a single-account setup is acceptable only for testing [1].
keyFacts: Recommends two accounts: a separate issuing account and a distribution account.
The issuing account creates supply and manages authorization flags.
The distribution account is public-facing and sends assets to users.
avoid: Do NOT claim a single account is the recommended/canonical issuing pattern for production assets.
Do NOT claim Stellar assets are deployed as ERC-20 / Solidity contracts.
Do NOT claim the issuing account holds a balance of its own asset.

Classic asset model basics. Dossier §1.1, §1.6. 'Best practice is to create two accounts when issuing an asset' (control-asset-access).

- The network **finds a path** through SDEX offers and/or AMM pools (e.g. USDC→XLM→EURC) and delivers EURC **atomically in one transaction**; the wallet never has to hold XLM or the intermediate hop asset [1].
- The **recipient must hold a trustline to the asset they receive (EURC)** for the payment to land; trustlines are required for non-native assets [1].
- Strict-receive bounds the EURC delivered while capping USDC spent via **`sendMax`** (strict-send instead fixes the USDC sent and sets a `destMin`). Settles in seconds for a low network fee [1].

The network finds a path through SDEX offers, AMM pools, or both.

cases.question: What is the Stellar Wallet SDK and which anchor SEP flows does it wrap?

golden.answer:
The **Stellar Wallet SDK** is SDF's **TypeScript library for building wallet apps** that consume
anchor flows, so a wallet integrates the anchor SEPs once rather than per-anchor [1]. It wraps the
**client-side** anchor flows: **SEP-6** (programmatic deposit/withdraw), **SEP-10** (auth),
**SEP-12** (KYC), **SEP-24** (hosted deposit/withdraw), and **SEP-38** (quotes) — plus **SEP-1**
discovery of the anchor [1][2]. It is the **wallet-side counterpart to the (Java) Anchor Platform**,
which is the **anchor backend**; the Wallet SDK is **not** anchor infrastructure itself. A wallet
built on it can interoperate with any compliant anchor without bespoke per-anchor integration.

Sources: [1] Stellar Wallet SDK documentation; [2] github.com/stellar/typescript-wallet-sdk.
keyFacts: Defines SDF's TypeScript Wallet SDK for Stellar wallet apps using anchor flows.
It wraps client-side SEP-1/6/10/12/24/38, not SEP-31.
avoid: Do NOT misnumber the SEPs it wraps.
Do NOT describe the Wallet SDK as anchor backend infrastructure (that is the Anchor Platform).
Do NOT claim the Wallet SDK wraps SEP-31.

cases.question: How does Circle CCTP V2 move native USDC to or from Stellar, and which fee claims must be checked live?

golden.answer: Circle's release notes record **Stellar mainnet support on 2026-05-18**, and SDF and Circle publicly announced CCTP live on Stellar on **2026-05-19**. The earlier **2026-02-24** date previously called the launch was not recoverable from accessible primary material, so do not collapse it with either confirmed May milestone. Stellar is CCTP domain 27. CCTP burns native USDC on the source and mints native USDC on the destination. For Stellar G-, M-, or C-address recipients, use Circle's CctpForwarder path; a wrong mintRecipient or destinationCaller can strand funds. Stellar USDC uses 7 decimals while CCTP messages use 6, so the seventh outbound decimal remains on Stellar. On 2026-07-11, Circle's fee endpoint returned Fast/Standard 0/0 for domain 27→0 and 1 bp/0 for 0→27; re-query /v2/burn/USDC/fees. Circle transfer fees are separate from network resources, relayer, integrator, and any swap charges.
keyFacts: Circle dates Stellar support to 2026-05-18 and the public-live announcement to 2026-05-19.
Use CctpForwarder with correct mintRecipient or destinationCaller for G/M/C funds.
The 6-decimal CCTP format leaves Stellar USDC's seventh decimal on Stellar.
Re-query /v2/burn/USDC/fees for 2026-07-11 Fast/Standard 27→0 0/0, 0→27 1 bp/0.
Treats Circle fees, network resources, relayers, integrators, and swaps as distinct costs.
avoid: CCTP locks USDC and issues a wrapped Stellar token.
Every CCTP route is permanently fee-free and exactly 1:1 after all costs.
Do NOT call 2026-02-24 the Stellar launch without accessible primary evidence or merge technical support and public announcement into one date.

cases.question: Walk me through the order of SEPs and controls a compliant Stellar anchor uses to onboard a customer and process a regulated deposit.

golden.answer:
There is no single universal compliance order independent of the product, account type, asset, and jurisdiction. A practical capability-driven flow is:

1. Discover the anchor's advertised services and endpoints through SEP-1 and its /info responses.
2. When an endpoint requires authentication, use **SEP-10 for G/M accounts** or **SEP-45 for C accounts**. SEP-12 always uses the applicable JWT; SEP-6 authentication is conditional; SEP-24 protects user-data endpoints.
3. If the client must provide KYC data directly, use **SEP-12 PUT /customer**. A SEP-24 hosted flow may collect information in the anchor UI instead.
4. Use **SEP-6** for a programmatic deposit/withdrawal or **SEP-24** for a hosted interactive flow, according to the advertised capability.
5. Only when the transferred classic asset is **SEP-8 regulated**, route the wallet-signed transaction to its separate approval server. SEP-8 requires **Authorization Required plus Authorization Revocable**; clawback is optional. The server signs/returns and the wallet submits.
6. Apply the legal, licensing, AML, sanctions, custody, and disclosure obligations that attach to the actual actors, activity, route, and jurisdiction. Stellar and Anchor Platform supply technical rails; they do not transfer or guarantee regulatory compliance.

Anchor Platform can implement several of these APIs, but its broad supported-SEP set is not a universal mandate for every anchor or deposit.
keyFacts: Scopes the SEP sequence by capability, account, asset, and jurisdiction.
Uses SEP-10 for G/M accounts or SEP-45 for C accounts when authentication is required.
Treats SEP-12 as KYC and SEP-6/24 as transfer flows.
Uses SEP-8 only for regulated assets with Required + Revocable and wallet submission.
Scopes legal duties by actor, activity, route, and jurisdiction.
avoid: Do NOT scramble SEP roles.
Do NOT claim every deposit universally follows SEP-10 then SEP-12 or that SEP-8 applies to every asset.
Do NOT substitute clawback for SEP-8's Revocable requirement.
Do NOT give categorical licensing/legal advice or claim Anchor Platform itself supplies compliance.
golden.notes:
Multi-hop how-to chaining SEP-10/12/24/8 + flags, verified against the individual SEP specs. Trap: scrambling SEP roles.
Also good if the answer: For regulated assets, a SEP-8 approval server gates the transaction before submission. | The asset's native flags (AUTH_REQUIRED / AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED) enforce control at the ledger. | The anchor (a regulated financial institution) runs off-chain AML/sanctions screening; licensing burden is the anchor's, not Stellar's.
Golden cites: developers.stellar.org anchor / Anchor Platform docs and the relevant SEP specs.
CORRECTION 2026-07-10: grade a capability-driven matrix, not one mandatory sequence. SEP-10 G/M and SEP-45 C are account-scoped; SEP-6 auth is conditional; SEP-12 uses PUT for upload; SEP-8 is only for regulated assets and requires Required + Revocable; legal duties are actor/activity/jurisdiction-specific.

cases.question: What asset authorization flags can a Stellar issuer set on a regulated token, and what does each one do?

golden.answer:
- **`AUTH_REQUIRED`** — the issuer must **approve a trustline** before an account can hold/receive the
  asset [1].
- **`AUTH_REVOCABLE`** — the issuer can **revoke/freeze** an existing trustline's authorization (downgrade
  to limited or remove it) [1].
- **`AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED`** — every subsequent trustline is clawback-enabled, letting the issuer **claw
  back / burn** the asset from any holder; the docs state this flag **requires `AUTH_REVOCABLE` to also be
  set** [1][2].
- **`AUTH_IMMUTABLE`** — **locks** the authorization flags (and blocks account merge) once set; finalizes
  the asset's governance posture [1].
- Flags are managed via the **`set_options`** operation (account-level) and **`set_trust_line_flags`**
  (per-trustline) [1].

Sources: [1] developers.stellar.org control-asset-access; [2] clawbacks guide.
keyFacts: AUTH_REQUIRED needs issuer approval before a holder's trustline receives or holds assets.
Lists AUTH_REVOCABLE (issuer can revoke/freeze an existing trustline's authorization).
AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED lets the issuer claw back or burn any holder's asset balance.
Lists AUTH_IMMUTABLE (locks the authorization flags / prevents further changes once set).
avoid: Do NOT invent flags that don't exist (e.g. 'AUTH_FROZEN', 'AUTH_KYC_REQUIRED').
Do NOT claim AUTH_IMMUTABLE lets the issuer still change flags afterward, or that clawback works without AUTH_REVOCABLE.

Canonical, verified vs control-asset-access docs. Four flags: AUTH_REQUIRED(0x1), AUTH_REVOCABLE(0x2), AUTH_IMMUTABLE(0x4), AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED(0x8). Docs confirm clawback flag 'requires that revocable is also set'. Trap: hallucinated flag names; missing the AUTH_REVOCABLE precondition.

cases.question: How does clawback work on Stellar, which protocol version and CAP introduced it, and why does it exist?

golden.answer:
- Clawback lets an **asset issuer burn a specified amount of a clawback-enabled asset from any holder's
  trustline (or claimable balance)** — without the holder's cooperation; the assets are **burned, not
  returned** to the issuer [1].
- Introduced by **CAP-0035 ("Asset Clawback") in Protocol 17** (activated ~2021-06-01) [1][2].
- The issuer must have set **`AUTH_REVOCABLE` first, then `AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED`** — only then are new
  trustlines clawback-eligible [1].
- It was **designed to help issuers meet securities/regulatory obligations** (revoke after fraud, error,
  or regulatory action) [1].
- Implemented via the **Clawback** and **Clawback Claimable Balance** operations (after enabling the flag
  with Set Options) [1]. It needs **no Soroban contract**, and **no arbitrary account** can claw back
  another's funds — only the issuer of that asset.

Sources: [1] developers.stellar.org clawbacks; [2] CAP-0035.
keyFacts: An issuer can burn a specified asset amount from any holding account.
The clawback does not require the holder's cooperation.
Clawback was introduced by CAP-0035 in Protocol 17.
Clawback requires the issuer's AUTH_REVOCABLE and AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED flags.

cases.question: What counterparty risk does clawback create for holders of a regulated Stellar asset, and is it a protocol vulnerability?

golden.answer:
- Clawback is an **intentional, issuer-only feature** of clawback-enabled assets — a **regulatory tool,
  not a protocol bug/exploit** [1].
- It exposes holders to **issuer-side counterparty risk**: the issuer can **burn the asset from a holder's
  balance** (e.g. after fraud, error, or a sanctions/regulatory action) [1].
- It applies **only** to assets explicitly issued with **`AUTH_REVOCABLE` + `AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED`**;
  **XLM and ordinary assets without the flag are not clawbackable**, and **no arbitrary account** can claw
  back another's funds — only that asset's issuer [1][2].
- Holders can **inspect an asset's flags** before trusting it.

cases.question: How do Stellar anchors handle Travel Rule and BSA/AML obligations, and what is FinClusive's 'Compliance as a Service' role?

golden.answer:
FinClusive currently markets Compliance as a Service, KYC/KYB and financial-crime-compliance orchestration, reusable FinCID/CDD credentials, and gateway connectivity that includes Stellar. Treat those as current operator product claims, not proof that the service guarantees legal compliance. FinClusive's operating provisions describe a third-party service-provider/payment-partner structure and say FinClusive is not itself a bank or licensed MSB; that is the company's current self-description, not an independent regulator determination.

A 2020 SDF article described a shared-verification model across multiple anchors and documented Biccos as a use case. That is dated historical context, not proof of current network-wide adoption. The audit did not verify MoneyGram, Bitso, Kado, or Nium as FinClusive CaaS partners, so they should not be listed as such.

Travel Rule, BSA/AML, licensing, custody, and sanctions duties depend on the covered actor, activity, transaction, route, threshold, and jurisdiction. Stellar is technical infrastructure, but it is also overbroad to say one entity called the anchor always carries every obligation. CaaS can support compliance workflows; it does not transfer or conclusively satisfy legal duties. This is not legal advice.

cases.question: If a regulated, clawback-enabled classic asset is used through the Stellar Asset Contract on Soroban, does it keep its authorization-flag and clawback semantics?

golden.answer:
Yes: using a classic issued asset through its deterministic Stellar Asset Contract does not create a control-free wrapped token or erase the asset's authorization/clawback model.

For a **G account**, balances and eligibility use the classic account/trustline ledger state: transfer requires an authorized line, and clawback requires the trustline's clawback-enabled flag. For a **C contract address**, the balance is stored in persistent ContractData rather than a classic trustline; that balance carries analogous authorized and clawback state derived and enforced by the SAC.

For an issued asset, the issuer is the **initial/default SAC admin**, but current admin can be delegated to another G or C address. After delegation, current-admin authorization controls privileged SAC operations. Native XLM is a separate exception with no admin. Thus the classic asset's control model remains relevant, but the issuer does not necessarily remain the current SAC admin forever.
keyFacts: SAC exposure preserves the same classic asset's authorization/clawback control model.
G accounts use classic trustline state.
C addresses use ContractData with analogous authorization/clawback fields.
Initial/default SAC admins are issuers for issued assets, with none for native XLM.
Current SAC admin may be delegated to a G or C address.
avoid: Do NOT claim SAC strips authorization or clawback controls.
Do NOT say every SAC balance is literally a classic trustline.
Do NOT conflate issuer, initial/default admin, and current delegated admin.
Do NOT assign an admin to native XLM.
golden.notes:
Verified vs SAC docs: 'Classic trustline semantics will be followed'; transfers succeed only if the trustline has AUTHORIZED_FLAG; clawback only works if the trustline has TRUSTLINE_CLAWBACK_ENABLED_FLAG; the asset issuer keeps administrative permissions. Confidence raised draft->high. Trap: claiming the SAC bypasses issuer controls.
Also good if the answer: The issuer's compliance controls (authorize, clawback) still apply to balances held/moved through the SAC.
Golden cites: developers.stellar.org Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) docs.
CORRECTION 2026-07-10: require the G-trustline versus C-ContractData split and initial/default versus current delegated admin distinction. Preserve the durable same-asset/control-model conclusion.

cases.question: In a SEP-6 programmatic deposit, which SEP actually carries the customer's KYC data — SEP-6 itself or another SEP?

golden.answer:
- **SEP-12 carries customer KYC data; SEP-6 does not define the KYC schema.** SEP-6 is the programmatic Deposit and Withdrawal API and uses SEP-12 PUT /customer when its flow requires client-supplied KYC.
- SEP-6 authentication is conditional and advertised through /info; when required, use SEP-10 for G/M accounts or SEP-45 for C accounts.
- SEP-24 is the hosted interactive alternative: the anchor UI may collect KYC, while protected user-data endpoints use the supported SEP-10/45 JWT. SEP-8 is a separate regulated-asset transaction approval standard.
keyFacts: SEP-12 carries KYC/customer data.
SEP-6 is the programmatic deposit/withdrawal API.
SEP-6 authentication is conditional.
SEP-12 uses account-appropriate SEP-10 or SEP-45 authentication.
Protected SEP-24 endpoints use account-appropriate SEP-10 or SEP-45 authentication.
avoid: Do NOT claim SEP-6 defines the KYC schema.
Do NOT claim every SEP-6/24 flow universally starts with SEP-10 or use SEP-10 for C accounts.
Do NOT claim SEP-6 carries KYC/customer data.
golden.notes:
Verified: SEP-12 is the 'KYC API' (carries the customer data); SEP-6 is the programmatic Deposit & Withdrawal API and relies on SEP-12 for KYC, with SEP-10 auth first. Trap: thinking SEP-6 carries the KYC schema itself.
Also good if the answer: In SEP-6 (programmatic, no hosted UI) the wallet collects and submits KYC via SEP-12; in SEP-24 the anchor's hosted flow collects it. | Both authenticate via SEP-10 first.
Golden cites: SEP-6 and SEP-12 specs / developers.stellar.org docs.

cases.question: How does SEP-8 let an issuer enforce compliance on a regulated asset, and what is the approval server's role in the transaction flow?

golden.answer:
- **SEP-8 is the Regulated Assets standard** for classic assets whose issuer requires per-transaction approval. The issuer sets both **Authorization Required and Authorization Revocable** and publishes regulated=true, approval_server, and approval_criteria in the asset's SEP-1 stellar.toml. **Clawback is separate and optional; it is not a SEP-8 prerequisite.**
- The wallet builds and signs a transaction, detects the regulated asset, and POSTs its encoded transaction to the approval server. The server checks policy and returns success, revised, pending, action_required, or rejected. Success adds issuer approval to the compliant transaction. A revised transaction must preserve user intent, be inspected, and be re-signed by the wallet.
- After all required signatures are present, **the wallet submits the transaction**. The approval server does not submit it. This is a classic-asset authorization flow and does not require Soroban.
keyFacts: Names SEP-8 as the Regulated Assets standard.
SEP-8 requires Authorization Required/Authorization Revocable, with optional clawback.
It requires regulated, approval_server, and approval_criteria stellar.toml fields.
Wallet duties include signed-transaction posting and five approval statuses.
Wallet duties include revision re-signing and final-transaction submission.
avoid: Do NOT call SEP-8 KYC or authentication.
Do NOT substitute AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED for SEP-8's AUTH_REVOCABLE requirement.
Do NOT say the approval server submits the transaction or omit wallet inspection/re-signing of revisions.
Do NOT claim Soroban is required.
golden.notes:
Canonical on-chain mechanic. Verified vs SEP-0008: title 'Regulated Assets'; the Approval Server 'receives a signed transaction, checks for compliance, and signs it on success' (the wallet then submits). Trap is conflating SEP-8 (regulated assets) with SEP-12 (KYC)/SEP-10 (auth).
Also good if the answer: The regulated asset is configured so transfers require issuer approval (authorization gating), tied to the asset's authorization flags. | WisdomTree-style issuers used SEP-8 to create assets that require issuer approval to transact, without a smart contract.
Golden cites: The SEP-8 spec (stellar-protocol GitHub) or developers.stellar.org regulated-assets docs.
CORRECTION 2026-07-10: mandatory flags are Required + Revocable. Clawback is optional. The approval server signs/returns; the wallet inspects and re-signs revised transactions and submits the final transaction.

cases.question: What happened in the YieldBlox/Reflector oracle-manipulation incident, roughly how much was lost/recovered, and what are the design lessons?

golden.answer:
On **February 22, 2026**, after setup beginning late February 21, an attacker manipulated the thin USTRY/USDC Stellar DEX market from roughly $1.06 to about $106. Reflector Pulse's five-minute volume-weighted market feed published the manipulated value in two fresh rounds, which passed the YieldBlox pool's adjacent-round max_dev=10 check. The community-managed YieldBlox Blend V2 pool then accepted the value as collateral. No compromise of Reflector contracts, Blend core, Etherfuse's issuer contract, Stellar consensus, or Stellar core was established; the failure chain was market quality, feed methodology, and pool/oracle-consumer configuration and exposure.

The two exploit transactions transferred **61,249,278.3064502 XLM** and **1,000,196.7040837 USDC**. A decoded pre-transaction state shows an existing roughly 14,000 USDC liability; the reviewed live sources did not establish that amount as a separate exploit borrow, so do not add it to the exploit transfer as a single **1,014,196.7040837 USDC** gross-borrow claim. Do not turn the token quantities into a settled dollar loss: the PoC values them at about **$10.86M** at incident-time prices, while Blockaid, BlockSec and other reports use different dated valuations and definitions. The prior claim that Script3 later estimated about **$10.5M net loss** could not be confirmed from accessible primary material and is not retained as verified.

About **48M XLM** was quarantined through coordinated validator transaction filtering; Blockaid attributes 48,069,094 XLM. Quarantine means identified accounts could not originate accepted transactions—it is not repayment, a rollback, or recovered funds. Script3's remediation repository and dated notices show direct supplier remediation on **February 27** and backstop remediation on **March 20**, with small-value/nonexistent-account handling and liquidated-user exclusions. The reviewed evidence does not prove attacker-held funds were returned.

Design lessons are layered: timestamp checks remain necessary but were not causal here because the poisoned values were fresh; require independent value/NAV bounds, market-depth and active-trader minimums, robust multi-window aggregation, longer clean baselines, per-asset supply/borrow/value caps, isolation and circuit breakers, pool-ice and migration paths, and first-anomaly monitoring. A TWAP/VWAP may be one layer, but the incident does not prove that TWAP alone would have prevented the drain.
keyFacts: Dates the YieldBlox Blend V2 USTRY-SDEX/Reflector 5-minute-VWAP drain to 2026-02-22.
Reports 61,249,278.3064502 XLM and 1,000,196.7040837 USDC as exploit transfers.
Treats the 14,000 USDC liability as pre-existing and all valuations as source-specific.

cases.question: What does it take to become a Stellar anchor, including SEP and Anchor Platform setup, licensing, liquidity or float, and on-ramp/off-ramp operating requirements?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the current official Stellar documentation, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Becoming an anchor has separate technical, operating, and legal workstreams. Technically, publish SEP-1 discovery and implement only the services you offer: SEP-6 or SEP-24 for ramps, SEP-10 for G/M authentication and SEP-45 for C accounts where applicable, SEP-12 when client-driven customer data is required, SEP-31 for receiving cross-border payments, and SEP-38 for quotes. Anchor Platform can supply plumbing but does not confer permission or licensing.

For the legal perimeter, identify each legal entity, country/customer nexus, asset and legal issuer, and who accepts/transmits/exchanges/issues/redeems/custodies value. Then assess the applicable federal registration, state money-transmitter, bank/payment/e-money/CASP, agent/exemption, sanctions, consumer, privacy, and safeguarding rules. In the US, federal MSB registration and state licensing are distinct; in the EU, EMT issuance, crypto-asset services, and payment/money-remittance services are separate classifications. The answer depends on facts and jurisdiction—obtain local counsel.

Operationally, demonstrate banking/payout access, liquidity and settlement capacity, reconciliation, support, security, KYC/sanctions processes, and incident handling. Settlement capacity may be own prefunding, payout-partner credit, JIT liquidity, or another documented arrangement; do not hard-code one model.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.

cases.question: What's the difference between custodial and non-custodial wallets on Stellar, and how should a remittance or SEP-31 app choose between them?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer derives its named examples and status claims from the live Stellar Scout directory or research data, then dates the roster so it is not presented as permanent. As of 2026-07-11, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Custodial means the provider controls signing/key custody or maintains an internal ledger that lets it move user funds. Non-custodial means the user controls signing authority and the app cannot move funds without user authorization. On Stellar, the same remittance UX can be built either way, but the risk allocation changes: custodial designs improve recovery/support and simplify some payout operations while increasing custody, safeguarding, recordkeeping, licensing, and operational-liability burdens. A non-custodial design does not by itself determine a regulated remittance business's duties. Apply each relevant jurisdiction's rules to the activities performed. Where the business is an obliged entity, plan for applicable AML/CFT, sanctions, and travel-rule controls. Plan fraud and customer-support operations separately.

For SEP-31/cross-border apps, choose the custody model around the anchor and payout flow: who authenticates through SEP-10, who submits KYC through SEP-12, who funds the Stellar payment, who handles memos/muxed-account bookkeeping, who can refund or remediate failed payouts, and who is responsible if the user loses keys. The MoneyGram Access guide shows this distinction explicitly by describing custodial and non-custodial authentication patterns for SEP-10/SEP-24 integration.

Examples must be dated and sourced. Scout currently lists Decaf as a non-custodial wallet for cross-border money movement using Stellar/Solana and MoneyGram/partner ramps, while the official TypeScript Wallet SDK is a build tool, not a custody provider. Do not label a wallet or custody vendor by marketing category alone.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.
keyFacts: Presents specific current or dated source evidence, not unsupported memory.
Makes the as-of date visible for every changeable roster, status, version, or measurement.
Defines custody by provider or user control of keys, signing, ledgers, and fund movement.
Applies compliance duties by activity and jurisdiction, not custody label.
Aligns SEP-31 custody with anchor/user auth, KYC, payout, and support ownership.
avoid: Do NOT label a wallet custodial or non-custodial without current evidence of its control model.
Do NOT say non-custodial design eliminates KYC/compliance obligations for regulated remittance flows.
Do NOT claim the observed live result set is a complete or permanent roster; explicitly historical facts remain historical.

cases.question: How do I export a complete Stellar account transaction history for tax or accounting, and what should I know about TurboTax or CoinTracker-style integrations?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the current official Stellar documentation, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

First determine the data source's retained range. Horizon pagination can enumerate the classic transactions, operations, and effects that **that Horizon instance still retains**, but reaching the final page does not prove all-time completeness. Check history_elder_ledger/provider retention and record the export's first and last ledger.

For complete historical coverage, use an archival/indexed source such as **Hubble/BigQuery**, a Galexie-derived data lake, or another provider that explicitly documents the needed history. RPC getTransactions scans a retained **ledger range**; it is not an account-history endpoint, and ordinary getTransactions/getEvents retention is not made all-time merely because getLedgers archival export exists.

Export more than payments: transactions, operations, effects/ledger-entry changes, fees, trades, claimable balances, and contract events as relevant. Decode XDR with a current SDK. Deduplicate/idempotently checkpoint by transaction/operation/event identity and reconcile classic plus contract activity.

Tax software is a separate, volatile provider workflow. As of 2026-07-10, CoinTracker documents CSV import for Stellar rather than direct sync; verify current format, jurisdiction, plan, and transaction limits. This is data-export guidance, not tax advice.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.

Requires operations, effects, events, and fees beyond payments in a reconciled export.

Do NOT call RPC getTransactions account-filtered or all-time because getLedgers archival export exists.

The SEP also contains an expressly **non-normative claim-based reference appendix** where functions such as add_identity appear. Separately, OpenZeppelin's current stellar-contracts RWA suite implements concrete identity registries/profiles, compliance modules, manager roles, pause/freeze/recovery, and examples. Those library helpers and authorization boundaries are implementation APIs, not automatically the SEP's stable core interface.

Pin both the SEP and library commit before copying signatures. Current hosted docs/examples still contain older can_transfer/can_create wording while v0.3 source uses Transferred/Created/Destroyed hooks. Treat source/spec at the selected commit as controlling. Stellar classic flags, clawback, SEP-8, and SAC remain separate mechanisms. None of these contracts creates securities-law, custody, disclosure, transfer-agent, or off-chain-rights compliance.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.

cases.question: I want to build a cross-border payment or remittance business on Stellar; which stablecoin and SEP rails should I use, and how should I structure corridors with on- and off-ramps?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer derives its named examples and status claims from the live Stellar Scout directory or research data, then dates the roster so it is not presented as permanent. As of 2026-06-29, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Stellar can be a good settlement layer for a remittance business because it gives fast settlement, standardized anchor protocols, and liquid stablecoin rails, but it is not a complete remittance company by itself. A real corridor needs: source on-ramp, customer onboarding/KYC, settlement asset, FX/quote path, destination off-ramp, liquidity/float, sanctions/fraud controls, reconciliation, refunds, customer support, and legal/compliance coverage in each jurisdiction.

Map rails to the job. SEP-1 lets wallets discover anchor metadata; SEP-10 authenticates account control; SEP-12 handles KYC/customer data; SEP-24/SEP-6 handle deposit and withdrawal flows; SEP-31 handles cross-border payments; SEP-38 gives price/FX quotes. MoneyGram Access is an example of a USDC cash-in/cash-out integration using SEP-10 and SEP-24, not proof that every remittance corridor is available.

Stablecoin choice should be corridor-specific: use issuer quality, liquidity, redemption, geography, compliance fit, and anchor support rather than defaulting universally to XLM or one stablecoin. Most founders should first integrate existing anchors/ramp partners in a narrow corridor, measure quote quality and failure handling, and only become an anchor where owning licensing, payout rails, liquidity, and support creates an advantage.

cases.question: How do I deploy and operate the Stellar Disbursement Platform, and what recipient account types can it disburse to?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the current official Stellar documentation, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Current SDP is an open-source bulk-disbursement stack whose **Core implements native SEP-10 and SEP-24** and publishes its own stellar.toml endpoints; it does not require an external Anchor Platform. Dashboard/Admin APIs manage tenants and disbursements, Core queues/coordinates payments, and TSS builds, submits, and monitors Stellar transactions.

Keep recipient models distinct:

- an external/classic wallet can register through SEP-24 and authenticate through SEP-10;
- the direct-payment API can pay an onboarded/recorded **G or C address** outside the batch-disbursement workflow;
- SDP can create an embedded passkey-controlled **C-address wallet**, using SEP-45 during SEP-24 and fee sponsorship for relevant transactions.

Current public recipient/direct validators accept encoded G or C addresses and reject encoded M-address strings. A G address plus ID memo may support pooled/custodial routing, but that is not the same as accepting M encoding. Sponsorship is a transaction/fee property, not another address type. Do not promise undocumented arbitrary pooled-ledger semantics.

cases.question: How can an individual or small business tokenize a real-world asset on Stellar, and what legal structuring and compliance issues should they consider?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the live Stellar Scout directory or research data, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Minting a Stellar asset or contract token does **not** by itself create ownership, priority, redemption, or enforcement rights in a house, bond, receivable, commodity, carbon unit, or other off-chain asset. First classify the asset and jurisdiction, then map the legal rights.

Document the underlying owner/custodian; governing contract, prospectus, title or registry; official master ownership record; holder entitlement and bankruptcy priority/remoteness; servicing, insurance, defaults, transfers, redemptions, and enforcement. The structure might use an issuer entity, SPV, trust, fund, title/warehouse registry, custodian entitlement, contractual/synthetic claim, or another model—none is universal. The token may be the authoritative issuer-sponsored record, a notification that updates an off-chain master record, a custodial entitlement token, or may convey no underlying right.

Stellar controls such as Authorization Required/Revocable, clawback, SEP-8 approval, SAC, or OpenZeppelin/SEP-57 contracts can enforce a policy already defined by the legal structure. They do not create title, legal compliance, or bankruptcy protection. Use current primary law and issuer documents, disclose the exact rights and risks, and obtain counsel. Institutional examples such as BENJI illustrate one transfer-agent/system-of-record model, not a copyable template.

cases.question: How do x402, MPP, AP2, and ACP compare for agent payments, and which are Stellar-specific vs general?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer derives its named examples and status claims from the current source data named by the case, then dates the roster so it is not presented as permanent. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

All four are **general/external protocols or commerce layers**; none is intrinsically a Stellar standard. Their Stellar relationship differs:

- **x402:** an open HTTP-402 payment protocol created at Coinbase and now governed through the x402 Foundation/Linux Foundation ecosystem. Stellar has an available x402 scheme using signed Soroban authorization entries, a facilitator, and SEP-41 tokens such as USDC.
- **MPP (Machine Payments Protocol):** a payment-method-agnostic Challenge–Credential–Receipt protocol. General MPP supports charge, session, and subscription intents; it is not streaming-only. The draft Stellar method supports one-time SEP-41 charge transfers and optional session/channel work.
- **AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol):** an emerging authorization/commerce protocol built around signed mandates and moving through FIDO standardization. x402 is an optional extension/composition path, not a required AP2 settlement route.
- **ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol):** a beta checkout/commerce interaction protocol. It delegates payment to compatible handlers/PSPs and is not a Stellar-native settlement rail.
- **SEP-41:** Stellar's Soroban Token Interface and the token substrate used by Stellar x402/MPP implementations. It does not turn x402 or MPP into SEPs and does not apply to AP2/ACP as whole protocols.

Use dated maturity terms: available integration, beta, Draft/Internet-Draft, proposed, or emerging are not interchangeable.

cases.question: Can I run a profitable arbitrage, path-payment, or market-making bot on Stellar with small capital, and how do strict-send/strict-receive path queries work?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the current official Stellar documentation, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-11, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Stellar supports path payments through `PathPaymentStrictSend` and `PathPaymentStrictReceive`. Path payments can traverse orderbook and pool liquidity. The protocol provides execution mechanics and a 0.3% AMM fee to liquidity providers, but it does not guarantee arbitrage or market-making profit. Profitability depends on live prices, liquidity, slippage, transaction fees, latency, competition, and capital. A strict-send quote fixes the source amount and estimates destination output, then the submitted transaction should protect the user with `destination_min`; a strict-receive quote fixes destination amount and protects the sender with `send_max`. If liquidity moves before inclusion, the operation can fail with path-payment result codes such as `UNDER_DESTMIN`, `OVER_SENDMAX`, or no usable path / too-few-offers. Sources: Stellar path-payment guide and Horizon operation-specific result-code docs.

For a small-capital bot, the defensible answer is "possible to build, not reliably profitable." Expected costs and risks include spreads, slippage, base fees and surge pricing, failed transactions, stale quotes, minimum reserves/trustlines, path disappearance, competition, latency, inventory imbalance, and thin pools. Backtesting and testnet/paper trading are required before risking funds; Raven should not recommend a strategy as a guaranteed return.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.

Profitability is intentionally not gated on a current numeric estimate; Phase 3 should attack any answer that turns pathfinding mechanics into financial advice.

cases.question: What is Franklin Templeton's BENJI token on Stellar and what fund does it represent?

golden.answer:
**BENJI** is the **share token of Franklin Templeton's Franklin OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund
(FOBXX)** on Stellar [1]. FOBXX was the **first US-registered mutual fund to use a public blockchain
(Stellar) as its official system of record** for recording share ownership and processing
transactions; it has been **live on Stellar since 2021** [1]. The fund holds **at least ~99.5% of
assets in US government securities** (cash and repos fully collateralized by US gov securities) [2], and
BENJI is notable for **intraday yield and peer-to-peer (P2P) transferability of shares** [1]. Franklin
also marked the **5-year BENJI milestone (Apr 30, 2026)** and shipped the first Luxembourg UCITS (2024)
and first Singapore retail tokenized fund (2025) on Stellar [1].

Sources: [1] stellar.org BENJI 5-year press release; [2] Franklin Templeton FOBXX product page.

cases.question: What is Blend on Stellar and who builds it?

golden.answer: **Blend** is a Soroban lending/borrowing protocol that lets users deploy permissionless, isolated pools, supply assets, and take over-collateralized loans. Official docs describe the immutable base protocol as having **no DAO or central operator**, but that does not make every pool governance-free: pool creators choose assets, owner/management strategy, oracle, backstop take, and risk parameters, and a pool can be owned/mutable or governed through a separate contract. Describe Blend as an important lending primitive without requiring an unsupported timeless dominance or Aave-equivalent ranking.

cases.question: If I have USDC on Ethereum in MetaMask, what is the safest way to bridge to Stellar, and how does Axelar's security model compare with other Stellar bridges?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the live Stellar Scout directory or research data, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

There is no provider-independent 'safest bridge.' For Ethereum **Circle USDC → canonical Stellar USDC**, first verify a current native-burn/mint or native-liquidity route rather than assuming an Axelar label gives the same asset. On **2026-07-10**, tested routes differed:
- Allbridge Next used **Circle CCTP** and delivered canonical Stellar USDC.
- Allbridge Core used its native-liquidity/message path and also selected canonical Stellar USDC.
- Squid's canonical-USDC quote used an **Intents/RFQ** provider, not Axelar.
- An explicit Axelar quote delivered **USDC.axl**, a different contract representation—not Circle-native Stellar USDC.

CCTP burns/mints native USDC; Axelar uses a validator/gateway interchain trust model; Allbridge Core adds liquidity-pool and messaging dependencies. Re-quote at execution time, inspect the messenger and destination issuer/SAC, verify fees/limits and Circle forwarder fields, use a Stellar destination address, and send a small test. MetaMask can be the EVM source wallet, but this audit did not verify MetaMask Bridge itself as the Stellar route. None of these observations is a safety guarantee.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.

cases.question: Since XLM has no native protocol staking, how can I build a staking or yield feature for my own Soroban token?

golden.answer:
XLM does not have native protocol staking rewards. Stellar reaches consensus with SCP/FBA rather than proof-of-stake, and official docs state validators do not receive monetary rewards. A "staking" product for a Soroban token is therefore an application/protocol feature: the contract must define the deposited token, reward source, lock/accounting rules, emission schedule, withdrawal/claim flow, admin controls, and failure behavior.

The building blocks can include SEP-41 custom contract tokens, Stellar assets exposed through the Stellar Asset Contract, AMM liquidity incentives, vault/reward-distributor contracts, or lending/yield protocols such as Blend. The answer must distinguish staking-language from lending, liquidity mining, fixed yield, and points/rewards. It should name sustainability, securities/compliance, smart-contract, oracle/pricing, and disclosure risks, and require audits plus staged testnet/mainnet launch for user funds.
keyFacts: States XLM does not have native protocol staking rewards like proof-of-stake chains.
Implements custom-token staking or yield at the application, contract, or protocol layer.
Defines the reward source, lock and accounting rules, and withdrawal logic.
Names Soroban tokens, SAC tokens, Blend/lending, AMMs, vaults, or reward distributors.
Matches each primitive and its risks to the design.
avoid: Do NOT imply users can earn native XLM staking rewards from the Stellar protocol.
Do NOT promise yield without identifying a real reward source and risks.
golden.notes:
No unresolved factual caveat; compliance/yield-risk treatment is jurisdiction- and product-specific.
Also good if the answer: Discusses reward sustainability, securities/compliance, smart-contract risk, oracle/pricing risk, and user disclosure. | Distinguishes staking terminology from lending, liquidity mining, and fixed-yield products.

cases.question: As a retail user, how do I provide liquidity to Stellar AMM or DeFi pools, compare yields across protocols, and understand impermanent-loss and withdrawal risk?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer derives its named examples and status claims from the live Stellar Scout directory or research data, then dates the roster so it is not presented as permanent. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

Start by identifying the exact venue and asset contracts/issuers. For a **classic Stellar constant-product pool**, establish the asset trustlines and pool-share trustline, submit `LiquidityPoolDeposit` with price bounds/minimums, retain the non-transferable pool shares, and later use `LiquidityPoolWithdraw` for a pro-rata redemption; classic pools charge the protocol-defined swap fee. For a **Soroban venue or vault**, review/approve the exact contract flow and verify admin/upgrades, reward contracts, oracle/keeper dependencies, lock or withdrawal queues, and current UI-contract provenance—mechanics are not interchangeable.

Compare returns in separate dated components: swap-fee APR, reward-token emissions, lending/vault yield, and costs/slippage. **Impermanent loss** is LP underperformance versus simply holding the two reserve assets after their relative price changes; withdrawing realizes that relative outcome, and fees/incentives may or may not offset it. Check pool depth, volume, asset/issuer risk, contract/admin risk, oracle/keeper risk, reward-token price, lock/queue terms, and whether exits currently work. Use small test amounts. Never treat APY/TVL or withdrawals as guaranteed.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.
keyFacts: Dates each source-supported roster, status, version, measurement, or current observation.
Gives a venue-specific deposit/withdraw checklist.
Treats Classic pool-share operations and Soroban contract/vault flows as distinct.
Covers liquidity, issuer, contract/admin, oracle/keeper, and reward-token risks.
Covers lock/queue and withdrawal risks.
avoid: Do NOT promise returns, freeze APY/TVL, or assume all Stellar LP venues share the same deposit/withdraw mechanics.
Do NOT describe impermanent loss as a guaranteed permanent loss before comparing the LP position with holding and accounting for fees/incentives.
Do NOT claim the observed live result set is a complete or permanent roster; explicitly historical facts remain historical.
golden.notes:
Do not preserve any APY/TVL number without a date. Phase 3 should re-check protocol UIs/DeFiLlama if a numeric yield/TVL claim appears. cases.question: What is Reflector and how does the price oracle work on Stellar?

golden.answer:
**Reflector** is a Stellar/Soroban oracle and data-feed system. Provider nodes independently calculate values from Stellar Classic/Soroban markets and external market/FX source classes, build matching transactions, and exchange signatures; only matching transaction hashes aggregate. As of **2026-07-10**, its three public mainnet feeds (Stellar DEX/USDC, external USD markets, and FX/USD) were deployed and updating. Their admin accounts used seven shared weight-1 signers with threshold four, and recent updates carried four signatures. Treat that as the observed implementation, not a timeless security guarantee.

Public price feeds are described as free and expose SEP-40-style oracle interfaces. Do not extend that into an absolute claim of no limits or no possible paid service: Reflector also documents subscriptions/webhooks and governance can change terms. Exact upstream venues/weights, operator roster, deployments, and integration roster are freshness-sensitive. No reproducible evidence establishes a universal 'most-integrated' ranking.

cases.question: What is x402 on Stellar and how does it let APIs or AI agents charge per request?

golden.answer:
A grounded answer consults the current source data named by the case, directly answers the question with source-supported content, and dates any version-, provider-, or availability-sensitive claim. As of 2026-07-10, the verified sources supported this observed answer:

x402 is a general HTTP 402 payment protocol created by Coinbase Developer Platform and contributed to the Linux Foundation. On Stellar, the canonical scheme is **x402 v2 exact** on `stellar:testnet`/`stellar:pubnet`. The client builds a SEP-41 token `transfer(from,to,amount)` invocation, simulates it, and signs Soroban authorization entries; a classic asset participates through its SAC contract interface. USDC is the default, not the only token.

The resource server sets price and payee. A facilitator verifies structure, recipient, amount, authorization, expiration, and safety; settlement must reverify, rebuild with the facilitator source, sponsor fees, sign, and submit. The facilitator is not the seller and does not set the price. Current exact-v2 Stellar settlement is fee-sponsored. Coinbase-hosted Stellar support is documented testnet-only; OpenZeppelin documents testnet and mainnet hosted endpoints.

x402 can remove a buyer's traditional API subscription/account prerequisite, but hosted facilitator setup can still require service credentials: unauthenticated OpenZeppelin `/supported` probes returned 401 on **2026-07-10**, and official docs describe key issuance. x402 is distinct from MPP Charge/Session. As of 2026-07-10 the x402 Foundation listed membership tiers and SDF as Premier, while the Linux Foundation page still said the Governing Board was not seated; call organizations members, not seated governors.

The dated example is illustrative: a later grounded answer should report what the same source basis supports at its own observation time while preserving the stable distinctions above.
keyFacts: Presents source-supported content as a current or dated observation, not a memory claim.
Makes the as-of date visible for every changeable roster, status, version, or measurement.
Covers HTTP 402, Stellar v2 exact, SEP-41/SAC authorization, and facilitator settlement.
Qualifies protocol UX versus hosted facilitator API keys.
Distinguishes x402 from MPP.
avoid: Do NOT say x402 is Stellar-invented, supports v1 on Stellar, or directly pays classic assets without the SAC.
Do NOT claim x402 or hosted facilitator setup categorically never needs API keys.
Do NOT conflate the seller/payee, facilitator, price setter, x402, and MPP roles.
Do NOT present version-, provider-, interface-, or availability-sensitive observations as timeless; date the changeable part without weakening stable protocol or historical facts.
